summary: Psalm 34 begins with David-associated praise after escape, then invites others to join in magnifying Yahweh. The speaker moves from personal testimony of being heard and delivered to instruction about fearing Yahweh, speaking truth, doing good, seeking peace, and trusting that Yahweh hears the righteous and redeems his servants.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how praise, testimony, and wisdom instruction can be woven together in one poem. Inside Book I of Psalms, it joins personal distress to a broader lesson about refuge, righteousness, and God’s care for those who cry out.

context.author: The heading says “By David,” and links the psalm with an episode before Abimelech; such headings are ancient but their exact force is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms for prayer and teaching.
context.date: The Psalter is a collection formed over time; this individual psalm cannot be dated securely from its wording and heading alone.
context.setting: Book I of Psalms, a section dominated by David-associated prayers of distress and confidence.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, here combining praise, thanksgiving testimony, and wisdom instruction.

outline.heading: Praise that invites others
outline.note: The speaker blesses Yahweh continually, says the humble will be glad, and calls others to exalt Yahweh together.

outline.heading: Rescue remembered
outline.note: The speaker and the poor man cry out, Yahweh hears, and deliverance is described with the image of Yahweh’s angel encamping around those who fear him.

outline.heading: Invitation to trust
outline.note: The psalm invites readers to taste and see Yahweh’s goodness, fear him, and trust that those who seek him will not lack any good thing.

outline.heading: Instruction in the fear of Yahweh
outline.note: The teacher addresses children and connects life with truthful speech, turning from evil, doing good, and pursuing peace.

outline.heading: Yahweh hears and opposes
outline.note: Yahweh is attentive to the righteous and near to the brokenhearted, while his face is against those who do evil.

outline.heading: Affliction, judgment, and refuge
outline.note: The righteous may have many afflictions, but the psalm ends by contrasting the fate of the wicked with the redemption of Yahweh’s servants.

keyVerses.text: I sought Yahweh, and he answered me, and delivered me from all my fears.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the personal testimony that drives the psalm’s praise.

keyVerses.text: Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.
keyVerses.why: This is the psalm’s central invitation: the speaker asks others to discover Yahweh’s goodness by taking refuge in him.

keyVerses.text: Depart from evil, and do good. Seek peace, and pursue it.
keyVerses.why: This verse turns the psalm’s trust into concrete instruction about conduct.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart, and saves those who have a crushed spirit.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the psalm’s comfort for people who cry out from distress.

themes: Yahweh hears the cry of the righteous
fear of Yahweh as taught wisdom
judgment on evil and redemption of servants

questions.question: Why does the first line mention David and Abimelech?
questions.answer: The chapter begins with a heading that associates the psalm with David pretending to be insane before Abimelech, being driven away, and departing. Headings are ancient features of the Psalter, but readers differ on whether each one functions as authorship, association, dedication, collection notice, or remembered setting. The poem itself then moves immediately into praise and testimony.

questions.question: Who are “the humble” in this psalm?
questions.answer: Verse 2 says the humble hear the speaker’s boast in Yahweh and are glad. Within this chapter, they belong with the poor man who cries and is heard, those who fear Yahweh, the righteous who cry, and those with a broken heart or crushed spirit. The term points to people who receive the testimony as good news rather than as self-display.

questions.question: What does it mean to “magnify Yahweh”?
questions.answer: Verse 3 is an invitation to praise Yahweh together. The speaker is not making Yahweh larger in himself, but calling the community to recognize and exalt his name. The chapter begins as personal praise, but it quickly becomes shared praise.

questions.question: Does the psalm promise that faithful people will never suffer?
questions.answer: No. Verse 19 says, “Many are the afflictions of the righteous,” so the chapter plainly expects trouble for righteous people. Its claim is that Yahweh hears, is near, delivers, and redeems; it does not say the righteous avoid every hardship.

questions.question: What is “the fear of Yahweh” here?
questions.answer: Verse 11 says the speaker will teach “the fear of Yahweh,” and verses 13-14 immediately explain that instruction through speech and conduct: keep from evil speech, depart from evil, do good, seek peace, and pursue it. In this chapter, fearing Yahweh is not mere panic; it is reverent trust that shapes behavior.

questions.question: Who is “Yahweh’s angel” in verse 7?
questions.answer: The verse says that Yahweh’s angel encamps around those who fear him and delivers them. It does not explain the angel’s identity further. Later readers have debated angel language in Scripture, but this chapter’s direct point is protective deliverance around those who fear Yahweh.

questions.question: Why does the psalm talk about tongue and lips?
questions.answer: The instruction section makes speech part of a life that seeks good. Verse 13 says to keep the tongue from evil and the lips from speaking lies, and verse 14 pairs that with doing good and pursuing peace. The psalm treats truthful speech as one visible form of fearing Yahweh.

questions.question: Why is verse 20 important in later Christian reading?
questions.answer: In the chapter itself, verse 20 says Yahweh protects the righteous person’s bones so that not one is broken. Later Christian readers compare this verse with John 19:36, but that is reception beyond this psalm. Read first in Psalm 34, it belongs to the poem’s larger claim that Yahweh preserves and delivers the righteous amid affliction.

questions.question: How can Yahweh’s face be “against” people?
questions.answer: Verse 16 uses personal imagery to say Yahweh actively opposes those who do evil. This contrasts with verse 15, where Yahweh’s eyes and ears are toward the righteous and their cry. The image communicates attention and opposition, not a physical description of God.

glossary.def: The divine name used throughout this translation of the psalm for Israel’s God, the one praised, sought, feared, and trusted as refuge.
Those who hear the speaker’s praise and are glad; in the chapter they stand near the poor, afflicted, and brokenhearted who cry out to Yahweh.
People described as crying out to Yahweh, being heard by him, and facing many afflictions while still receiving deliverance.
Those contrasted with the righteous; the psalm says evil will kill them and that those who hate the righteous will be condemned.
A place of safety; in this psalm, taking refuge in Yahweh is linked with blessing and with not being condemned.
